title_en: The Beautiful Names of Allah — Al-Asma al-Husna
summary: The Beautiful Names of Allah (al-Asma al-Husna) are the divine names by which Allah described Himself in the Quran and Sunnah. Each name reveals an attribute of His perfection, and calling upon Him by these names is one of the most beloved forms of supplication.
content:
Allah has the most beautiful names — al-Asma al-Husna — and He commanded us to call upon Him by them: 'And to Allah belong the best names, so invoke Him by them' (7:180). These names are among the greatest means of knowing Allah, drawing close to Him through du'a, and cultivating the spiritual qualities that flow from recognising who He truly is.

## The Number: A Well-Known Hadith

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Allah has ninety-nine names — one hundred minus one — and whoever ihsa (encompasses/memorises/lives by) them will enter Jannah' (Bukhari 2736, Muslim 2677).

Important notes on this hadith:

1. The hadith does not say that Allah has only ninety-nine names. Classical scholars such as Ibn Taymiyyah emphasised this: the ninety-nine are a specific set of names memorising which is a means to Jannah, but Allah's names are not limited to ninety-nine. The Prophet (peace be upon him) supplicated: 'I ask You by every name that is Yours, which You named Yourself, or revealed in Your Book, or taught to any of Your creation, or kept in the knowledge of the unseen with You' (Ahmad — graded sahih).

2. The word 'ihsa' means more than memorisation: it means to know the names, understand their meanings, and live by their implications — praying to Allah by them and allowing them to shape one's conduct and relationship with Him.

3. The list of ninety-nine names appears in Tirmidhi (3507) via a chain that scholars have debated. The list itself is widely accepted as authentic in substance, though scholars note the specific number and sequence is not necessarily canonical. The Quran and Sahih Sunnah are the definitive sources for each individual name.

## Categories of the Names

The names are broadly categorised by their primary emphasis:

**Names of Majesty (Jalal):** Emphasise Allah's greatness, power, and independence — al-'Aziz (the Mighty), al-Jabbar (the Compeller), al-Mutakabbir (the Supreme), al-Qahhar (the Subduer), al-Qawi (the Strong).

**Names of Beauty (Jamal):** Emphasise His mercy, gentleness, and care — ar-Rahman (the Entirely Merciful), ar-Rahim (the Especially Merciful), al-Latif (the Subtle and Kind), al-Wadud (the Loving), al-Barr (the Beneficent).

**Names of Perfection (Kamal):** Encompass both — al-Hakim (the Wise), al-'Alim (the All-Knowing), al-Qadir (the Able), al-Sami' (the All-Hearing), al-Basir (the All-Seeing).

## Selected Names and Their Meanings

**Allah** — The proper name of God; the name from which all others derive. It is unique and has no plural or feminine form. It encompasses all attributes of divinity.

**ar-Rahman, ar-Rahim** — Both derive from the root rahma (mercy). Ar-Rahman is the vast mercy that encompasses all creation; ar-Rahim is the specific, enduring mercy directed to the believers. The Quran begins with both in the Basmalah.

**al-Hayy, al-Qayyum** — The Ever-Living, the Self-Sustaining who sustains all things. These are considered among the greatest of the names, found in Ayat al-Kursi (2:255), and the Quran's greatest verse.

**al-'Azim** — The Magnificent. Also in Ayat al-Kursi.

**al-Ahad** — The One, the Unique. The entire Surah al-Ikhlas (112) revolves around this concept: 'Say: He is Allah, the One; Allah, the Eternal Refuge; He does not beget, nor was He begotten; and there is none comparable to Him.'

**al-Ghafur, al-'Afuw** — The Forgiving, the Pardoning. Allah's forgiveness is one of the most frequently mentioned themes in the Quran. The Prophet taught the supplication: 'Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibb al-'afwa fa'fu 'anni' — O Allah, You are the Pardoner, You love to pardon, so pardon me (Tirmidhi 3513 — sahih).

## Living by the Names

Ibn al-Qayyim wrote that knowing Allah's names transforms the worshipper. To know Allah is al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) produces taqwa; to know He is al-Wadud (the Loving) produces hope and love in return; to know He is al-Qahhur (the Subduer) produces humility. The names are not theological abstractions — they are invitations to a living relationship.

The Quran instructs: 'He is Allah, the Creator, the Inventor, the Fashioner; to Him belong the best names. Whatever is in the heavens and earth exalts Him, and He is the Exalted in Might, the Wise' (59:24).
evidence_quran: Surah al-A'raf 7:180 — 'And to Allah belong the best names, so invoke Him by them'
Surah al-Baqarah 2:255 — Ayat al-Kursi: 'Allah — there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Self-Sustaining'
Surah al-Ikhlas 112:1-4 — 'Say: He is Allah, the One; Allah, the Eternal Refuge...'
Surah al-Hashr 59:22-24 — listing of divine names in closing verses
Surah Taha 20:8 — 'Allah — there is no deity except Him. To Him belong the best names'
evidence_hadith: Bukhari 2736, Muslim 2677 — 'Allah has ninety-nine names; whoever encompasses them will enter Jannah'
Tirmidhi 3507 — list of ninety-nine names (chain debated; content widely accepted)
Ahmad (sahih) — 'I ask You by every name that is Yours which You named Yourself or revealed in Your Book or kept in the knowledge of the unseen with You'
Tirmidhi 3513 (sahih) — supplication: 'Allahumma innaka 'afuwwun tuhibb al-'afwa fa'fu 'anni'
scholar_positions: The Athari position affirms all names as genuinely describing Allah's attributes, without metaphorical reinterpretation (ta'wil) of names that might seem problematic to reason. Ash'ari scholars apply ta'wil to certain attributes (such as 'hand' and 'face') while affirming the names. Maturidi scholars adopt a similar approach to Ash'ari. All three schools affirm the ninety-nine names and the obligation to call upon Allah by them. Ibn Taymiyyah's commentary on the names (in Majmu' al-Fatawa) remains a key Athari-tradition source.
